title: The complexity of matrix multiplication of two matrices and whose
subject: Algorithm
text: The complexity of matrix multiplication of two matrices A and B whose orders are m×n and n×p respectively is
solution:
Concept

The cost of standard (naive) matrix multiplication is governed by one rule: the work equals the number of entries in the product matrix multiplied by the work needed to fill each entry. Each output entry is a dot product over the shared (inner) dimension, so it costs a number of scalar multiply-add operations equal to that inner dimension.

Application

  1. A has order m×n and B has order n×p; multiplication is defined because A's column count (n) matches B's row count (n).

  2. The product C = A·B has order m×p, so it contains m·p entries that must be computed.

  3. Each entry C[i][j] is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B, taken over the shared dimension n: it needs n multiplications and n−1 additions, i.e. O(n) work.

  4. Total work = (number of entries) × (work per entry) = (m·p) × O(n) = O(m·n·p).

Cross-check

The triple-nested loop (over the m rows, the p columns, and the n shared terms) runs the inner statement m·n·p times, which confirms O(m·n·p). The product dimensions m and p and the shared dimension n each appear exactly once, with no squared factor — so no inner dimension is raised to a power.

optionFeedback.html: This expression accounts only for how many entries the product has and assigns no cost to producing any single entry, even though each entry is itself the result of combining a full row with a full column.

This expression carries an extra squared factor on the inner symbol that the multiplication procedure does not introduce; the inner symbol arising from the matching dimensions has no reason to be squared.
This expression carries an extra squared factor on the column symbol that the multiplication procedure does not introduce; the column symbol has no reason to be squared.
The value m×n×p is the product of the two outer dimensions and the one shared dimension, which is exactly the amount of work this multiplication requires.

solution: The Floyd-Warshall algorithm is the standard approach for finding all-pairs shortest paths in a weighted graph. title: The Floyd–Warshall algorithm for all-pair shortest paths computation is based
subject: Algorithm
text: The Floyd–Warshall algorithm for all-pair shortest paths computation is based on:
solution:
The Floyd–Warshall algorithm computes the shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in a weighted graph. It works by iteratively improving the shortest path estimates between vertices by considering each vertex as an intermediate point. The algorithm uses a dynamic programming approach, where the solution is built by solving smaller subproblems and reusing their results. It maintains a distance matrix that is updated in a triple loop, where each iteration considers one vertex as a potential intermediate node. This method ensures that all possible paths are considered, and the optimal substructure property is exploited to build the final solution.

title: Consider the following graph: Which one of the following is
subject: Algorithm
text:
Consider the following graph:

Which one of the following is NOT the sequence of edges added to the minimum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm?
solution:
Key idea: Kruskal's algorithm adds edges in non-decreasing order of weight, ignores loops, and skips any edge that would create a cycle. Ties (equal weights) may be broken arbitrarily, but every edge of a given smaller weight is considered before any larger-weight edge.

Relevant edge groups in increasing weight order (from the diagram):

  • Weight 1: loop (C,C) — ignored.

  • Weight 2: edges (T,D) and (B,D) — these are considered first; neither creates a cycle at that time so both will be added in some order.

  • Weight 3: edges (C,D) and (A,C) — considered after all weight-2 edges.

  • Higher weights: edges that connect any remaining vertices (for example (A,S) in the diagram) are considered later.

Application to the given sequences:

  • Any valid Kruskal ordering must place both (T,D) and (B,D) before edges of weight 3, unless adding one of them would already create a cycle. In this graph neither creates a cycle when first considered, so both appear among the earliest chosen edges.

  • The sequence (T,D),(D,C),(C,A),(A,S),(B,D) places (B,D) (a weight-2 edge) after weight-3 edges; this contradicts Kruskal's non-decreasing order, so that sequence is not possible under Kruskal.

  • The other listed sequences are consistent with Kruskal because they add the two weight-2 edges first (in some order), then the weight-3 edges, and finally the remaining connecting edge.

Conclusion: The sequence (T,D),(D,C),(C,A),(A,S),(B,D) is not a valid Kruskal order because it delays a smaller-weight edge until after larger-weight edges; the other provided sequences are possible.

optionFeedback.html: (T,D),(B,D),(C,D),(A,C),(S,A) is a valid Kruskal construction. Kruskal processes edges in non-decreasing order of weight (ignoring the loop). The two weight-2 edges (T,D) and (B,D) can be chosen in either order; neither creates a cycle at that time, so both will be added before any weight-3 edges. Adding (C,D) and (A,C) next (weight 3) and finally (S,A) connects the remaining vertex, producing a valid MST sequence.

(T,D),(D,B),(D,C),(C,A),(A,S) is also a valid Kruskal sequence. This lists the same set of edges as the previous sequence but with the two weight-2 edges in a particular order followed by the weight-3 edges. Ties between equal-weight edges can be broken arbitrarily, so this ordering is possible and yields the MST.

(T,D),(D,C),(C,A),(A,S),(B,D) is NOT a valid Kruskal sequence. The edge (B,D) has weight 2 and (C,D)/(A,C) have weight 3. Kruskal considers all weight-2 edges before weight-3 edges; since (B,D) does not create a cycle when first considered, it would be added earlier (among the weight-2 edges). Placing (B,D) after weight-3 edges contradicts the required non-decreasing weight order, so this ordering cannot occur under Kruskal.

(B,D),(D,T),(D,C),(C,A),(A,S) is a valid Kruskal ordering. It begins with the two smallest edges ((B,D) and (T,D), both weight 2) in some order, then takes the weight-3 edges ((C,D) and (A,C)), and finally connects the remaining vertex with (A,S). This ordering respects non-decreasing weights and avoids cycles.

title: Suppose that the minimum spanning tree of the following edge-weighted
subject: Algorithm
text:
Suppose that the minimum spanning tree of the following edge-weighted graph contains the edges with weights x, y, and z:

What is the maximum value of x + y + z?
solution:
Answer: 25

Key idea: Use the cut property (an edge can belong to some MST if it is a minimum-weight edge across some cut separating its endpoints). For each edge, pick a cut that isolates one endpoint's component and compare the other crossing edges to get an upper bound on the weight.

  • For the edge between F and G (weight x): consider the cut that isolates vertex F. The edges crossing that cut are A–F = 11 and F–G = x. To have the F–G edge included in some MST we need x to be at most the other crossing edge, so x ≤ 11.

  • For the edge between D and E (weight y): consider the cut that separates the pair {C,D} from the rest of the graph. The edges crossing that cut are C–H = 12, D–H = 9, D–I = 6, and D–E = y. The smallest competing crossing edge has weight 6, so to ensure D–E can be chosen in some MST we must have y ≤ 6.

  • For the edge between B and C (weight z): consider the cut that isolates vertex B. The edges crossing that cut are A–B = 13, B–G = 14, B–H = 8, and B–C = z. The smallest competing crossing edge has weight 8, so we must have z ≤ 8.

Therefore the maximum possible values that still allow those edges to appear in an MST are x = 11, y = 6, z = 8. The maximum sum is 11 + 6 + 8 = 25.

Achievability note: these bounds can be met simultaneously (ties in selection can be broken to include the specified edges). For example, with x = 11, y = 6, z = 8, Kruskal's algorithm can be ordered (or ties broken) so that the edges of weights 11, 6, and 8 are included in the resulting MST.

solution:
Concept — A spanning tree of a connected graph on n vertices is a cycle-free subgraph that keeps every vertex connected, and it always uses exactly n − 1 edges. Among all such trees, the minimum spanning tree is the one whose edge weights add up to the smallest total. Kruskal's algorithm builds it greedily: sort all edges by non-decreasing weight and accept an edge only when its two endpoints currently lie in different components; an edge whose endpoints are already joined would close a cycle and is rejected.

Application — The figure has 8 vertices (A to H) and 11 weighted edges, so any spanning tree of it must contain exactly 8 − 1 = 7 edges. Listing the edges in non-decreasing order of weight:

Applying Kruskal's rule to that sorted list:

  1. B–D (1): B and D lie in different components, so this edge is accepted.

  2. G–H (1): G and H lie in different components, so this edge is accepted.

  3. A–F (2): A and F lie in different components, so this edge is accepted.

  4. B–C (2): C joins the component {B, D}, so this edge is accepted.

  5. F–G (2): the component {A, F} merges with {G, H}, so this edge is accepted.

  6. A–B (3): the component {A, F, G, H} merges with {B, C, D}, so this edge is accepted. Six edges are now in place, with a running total of 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 11.

  7. C–H (3): C and H already lie in the same component, so this edge would close a cycle and is rejected.

  8. E–G (3): E is still isolated, so this edge is accepted. It is the seventh edge, and the total becomes 11 + 3 = 14.

  9. D–E (4), C–E (5) and E–H (6): all eight vertices are already connected by seven edges, so none of these is needed.

A lower bound agrees: the seven smallest edge weights anywhere in the figure are 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3 and 3, which already add to 14, so no seven-edge subgraph of this graph can cost less than 14.

Result — The minimum cost of a spanning tree of the given graph is 14.

title: Let be complete undirected graph on vertices, having edges with
subject: Algorithm
text: Let G be a complete undirected graph on 4 vertices, having 6 edges with weights 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. The maximum possible weight that a minimum weight spanning tree of G can have is:
solution:
Concept

A spanning tree of a connected graph on n vertices is a cycle-free subgraph that connects all n vertices using exactly n - 1 edges. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is the spanning tree of smallest total weight, and Kruskal's algorithm builds it by scanning edges from smallest weight to largest, adding an edge only if it joins two vertices that are not yet connected.

Cycle test (this answers the reported doubt): an edge creates a cycle precisely when both of its endpoints already lie in the SAME connected component formed by the edges chosen so far. We track components with a union-find (disjoint-set) structure: before adding an edge, ask whether its two endpoints share the same set root; if they do, adding the edge would close a loop, so it is skipped; if they differ, the edge is safe and we merge the two sets.

Here the question is a maximisation over assignments: the six weights 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 are not fixed to particular edges, so we may place them on the edges of the complete graph K4 to make the resulting MST as heavy as possible, then report that largest achievable MST weight.

Application

K4 has 4 vertices and 6 edges, so every spanning tree uses exactly 4 - 1 = 3 edges. To force the MST to keep heavier edges, we arrange the three smallest weights so they form a triangle among three of the vertices; Kruskal then has to discard one of them as a cycle, pulling in a heavier edge instead.

  1. Place weights 1, 2 and 3 on the three edges of one triangle, say on vertices A, B, C: edge A-B = 1, edge B-C = 2, edge A-C = 3.

  2. Kruskal scans in increasing order. It adds weight 1 (A-B): A and B are in different sets, so they merge.

  3. It adds weight 2 (B-C): C is in a different set from {A, B}, so it joins; now {A, B, C} is one component.

  4. It examines weight 3 (A-C): both A and C are already in the same component, so this edge would close a cycle and is skipped.

  5. The fourth vertex D is still unconnected, so the next smallest edge touching D is forced in. The smallest weight we can place on a D-edge is 4, giving D a connection of weight 4.

  6. Three safe edges are now chosen (1, 2 and 4) and all four vertices are connected, so the tree is complete with total weight 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.

Cross-check

Could a heavier MST exist? Whatever the assignment, Kruskal must take the weight-1 edge first (it can never form a cycle on its own) and the weight-2 edge second (two edges on four vertices cannot yet form a cycle). The third chosen edge is at best the weight-4 edge, because the weight-3 edge can be neutralised only by making 1, 2, 3 a triangle, which is exactly what we did. So no assignment beats 1 + 2 + 4. The maximum possible MST weight is therefore 7.

  • Larger sums like 15 (4 + 5 + 6) are impossible because Kruskal is always forced to take the weight-1 and weight-2 edges before any of the largest weights.

  • Summing all six edges (21) or near-total values describes the whole graph, not a 3-edge tree, so they overcount.

optionFeedback.html: The value 5 comes from leaving out an edge that the cycle test actually forces into the tree. Walk the union-find test edge by edge in increasing weight order: one more edge has to be admitted to connect the last vertex than this count assumes, so the construction here is incomplete.

A total of 8 comes from assuming one of the larger weights can be steered into the tree. But the lighter edges are admitted first and cannot be skipped, and no valid weight assignment lets the heavier edges all survive the cycle test, so a tree this heavy cannot be forced. Re-trace the edges with the union-find test to see which one is actually compelled in.

This total of 7 matches the construction in which 1, 2 and 3 are placed as a triangle so the weight-3 edge is rejected by the cycle test, forcing the next available edge to connect the last vertex. Because Kruskal must always take the two lightest edges first, this assignment yields the heaviest minimum spanning tree any arrangement of the weights can produce.

The value 20 (and similar near-total figures) sums almost every edge of the graph rather than a spanning tree. A spanning tree on four vertices keeps only three edges; admitting more would immediately fail the cycle test, so a total this large describes the full edge set, not a tree.

No answer was selected. Work through the edges in increasing weight using the union-find cycle test: keep an edge only when its endpoints lie in different components, and skip it when they are already joined. Tracking which edge is forced in to reach the last vertex leads you to the intended total.

title: Consider the following graph: Which of the following is/are represent
subject: Algorithm
text:
Consider the following graph:

Which of the following represents the sequence of edges added, in order, to build a minimum spanning tree using Prim's algorithm?
solution:
Concept

Prim's algorithm grows one connected tree from an arbitrary start vertex. At each step it adds the minimum-weight edge that crosses the cut between the in-tree vertices and the outside vertices, so the chosen edge always has exactly one endpoint already in the tree.

A sequence is a valid Prim order only if every listed edge actually exists in the graph, attaches a brand-new vertex (one endpoint inside the tree, one outside), and is the cheapest such crossing edge available at that moment.

Edges of this graph

a-b = 4, a-d = 3, a-c = 8, b-e = 9, b-d = 7, c-d = 5, d-f = 4, d-g = 3, d-h = 9, e-f = 5, e-h = 4. Note there is no edge between d and e.

Application (trace starting at vertex e)

  1. (e-h), weight 4: cheapest edge leaving {e} beats e-f (5) and b-e (9). Tree = {e, h}.

  2. (e-f), weight 5: cheapest crossing edge now; h offers no cheaper new edge. Tree = {e, f, h}.

  3. (d-f), weight 4: f-d (4) is the cheapest crossing edge. Tree = {d, e, f, h}.

  4. (d-a), weight 3: d-a (3) ties d-g (3); take a first. Tree = {a, d, e, f, h}.

  5. (d-g), weight 3: the remaining weight-3 crossing edge attaches g. Tree = {a, d, e, f, g, h}.

  6. (a-b), weight 4: cheapest crossing edge (vs d-c 5, d-b 7). Tree = {a, b, d, e, f, g, h}.

  7. (d-c), weight 5: attaches the last vertex c (cheaper than a-c 8). Tree = all 8 vertices.

The seven chosen edges span all 8 vertices and total 4 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 28, the minimum spanning tree weight.

Cross-check (why the other sequences fail)

  • Any sequence that lists edge d-e is invalid: there is no d-e edge in the graph, so it can never be a Prim step. Vertex e connects only via b-e (9), e-f (5), or e-h (4).

  • Any sequence that picks an edge whose both endpoints are still outside the current tree (for example taking e-f or e-h before either endpoint has joined) breaks Prim's single-connected-component growth.

  • Any sequence that takes a costlier crossing edge while a cheaper crossing edge is available (for example attaching c with d-c before bringing in b with the cheaper a-b) violates the greedy minimum-cut rule.

optionFeedback.html: This order brings vertex c into the tree at weight 5, but at that same moment a strictly cheaper crossing edge into the tree was still available and unused. Prim's algorithm can never pick a costlier crossing edge while a cheaper one is on offer, so taking the weight-5 step first breaks the greedy cut rule, and this order is not a valid Prim execution.

Reading this from start vertex e, every edge attaches a new vertex with the smallest available crossing weight: e-h (4), then e-f (5), then f-d (4), then d-a (3) and d-g (3), then a-b (4), and finally d-c (5) brings in the last vertex c. Each edge exists in the graph and each is the cheapest edge leaving the current tree, so these seven edges build the minimum spanning tree of total weight 28.

After the first three steps the tree is {a, b, d, g}. The next listed edge connects vertices e and f, but at that moment both e and f are still outside the tree. Prim can never add an edge whose two endpoints are both outside the current tree, because every new edge must touch the tree; this breaks single-component growth. The sequence also ends with (d-h) at weight 9, yet vertex h can be reached at weight 4, so (d-h) is not a minimum spanning tree edge at all.

The second listed edge (d-e) is not an edge of this graph at all: vertex d is joined only to a, b, c, f, g and h, and there is no direct connection between d and e. A Prim sequence can use only edges that actually exist, so a step that adds a non-existent edge can never occur. Vertex e itself connects only to b, f and h.

title: Let (V,E) be directed graph, where is the set of

text:
Let G (V,E) be a directed graph, where V={11,12,13,14,15,16} is the set of vertices and E is the set of directed edges, as defined by the following adjacency matrix A.

A[i][j]={1, 11≤ i ≤ j ≤ 16

A[i][j]={ 0, Otherwise A [i][j]=1 indicates a directed edge from node i to node j.

A directed spanning tree G, rooted at r∈V, is defined as a sub graph T of G such that the undirected version of T is a tree, and T contains a directed path from r to every other vertex in V. The number of such directed spanning trees rooted at vertex 11 is _______________
solution:
Answer: 120

Reasoning:

The adjacency matrix has A[i][j] = 1 for 11 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ 16, so there is a directed edge from a vertex p to a vertex q exactly when p ≤ q. (Self-loops p = q appear in the matrix but are not used as tree edges.) We count directed spanning trees (arborescences) rooted at vertex 11.

  • Vertex 12: its parent must be one of the earlier vertices {11} → 1 choice.

  • Vertex 13: its parent can be any of {11, 12} → 2 choices.

  • Vertex 14: its parent can be any of {11, 12, 13} → 3 choices.

  • Vertex 15: its parent can be any of {11, 12, 13, 14} → 4 choices.

  • Vertex 16: its parent can be any of {11, 12, 13, 14, 15} → 5 choices.

Each non-root vertex chooses its parent independently from the allowed earlier vertices, so the total number of directed spanning trees rooted at 11 is the product 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 × 5 = 120. Equivalently, for n = 6 vertices the count is (n−1)! = 5! = 120.

Note: The original solution used the term "MST" and gave an unclear sequence of examples. This improved solution gives a direct combinatorial count based on the adjacency rule.

title: Complete undirected graph is given on the vertex set to
subject: Algorithm
text: A complete undirected graph G is given on the vertex set 0 to (n – 1) for a fixed value of ‘n’. Draw the minimum spanning tree (MST) of a graph G, for the following cases and find the cost of MST: i) weight of the edge (u, v) is |u – v| ii) weight of the edge (u, v) is |u + v|
solution:
Case i — weight w(u,v) = |u - v|: The smallest possible positive weight is 1, which occurs for every pair of consecutive vertices (k, k+1). Choose the edges (0,1), (1,2), …, (n-2, n-1) to form a path connecting all vertices. Each chosen edge has weight 1, so the MST cost is 1 · (n-1) = n-1.

  • Example (n = 4): edges 0–1, 1–2, 2–3 each weight 1, MST cost = 3.

Case ii — weight w(u,v) = |u + v| = u + v (labels are nonnegative): For each vertex i > 0 the smallest edge incident to i is (0,i) with weight i. Taking all edges (0,1), (0,2), …, (0,n-1) yields a spanning tree (a star centered at 0) whose total cost is sum_{i=1}^{n-1} i = n(n-1)/2. No spanning tree can have smaller total cost because every vertex i>0 must be connected by some edge of weight at least i, and (0,i) achieves that minimum for each i.

  • Example (n = 4): edges (0,1)=1, (0,2)=2, (0,3)=3, MST cost = 1+2+3 = 6.

Final answer: For the weight |u-v| the MST cost is n-1. For the weight u+v the MST cost is n(n-1)/2.

optionFeedback.html: Correct. For weight |u-v| the smallest edges are between consecutive integers (0–1, 1–2, …, (n-2)–(n-1)), each of weight 1. The MST can be the path 0–1–2–…–(n-1) and its cost is 1 repeated (n-1) times, i.e. n-1. For weight u+v the MST is the star centered at vertex 0 using edges (0,i) of weight i, giving total cost sum_{i=1}^{n-1} i = n(n-1)/2.

Incorrect. The MST costs are not “none.” When edge weight is |u-v| you can connect consecutive vertices 0–1–2–…–(n-1) with edges of weight 1 each, so the MST cost is n-1. When edge weight is u+v, the MST is the star at vertex 0 with edges of weights 1,2,…,n-1, giving total n(n-1)/2.

Incorrect. The first cost is not (n-1)+1. For |u-v| the minimal edges have weight 1 between consecutive indices, so the MST cost is n-1 (not n). The second expression n^2/2 is not the precise integer formula; the correct cost for weight u+v is n(n-1)/2 (which equals n^2/2 - n/2).

Incorrect. The first cost is not n. For weight |u-v| the MST can be a path joining consecutive vertices, giving cost n-1 (one for each of the n-1 edges). The second part matches the correct cost for weight u+v, but the first part is incorrect.

title: How many minimum spanning tree(MST) are possible for given graph

text: How many minimum spanning tree(MST) are possible for given graph is____
solution:
Key insight: If the graph is the complete graph on 6 vertices and all edges have the same weight, then every spanning tree has the same total weight and therefore every spanning tree is a minimum spanning tree (MST).

  1. Count the vertices: there are 6 vertices (A, B, C, D, E, F).

  2. Count the edges: a complete graph on n vertices has n(n-1)/2 edges. For n = 6 this is 6×5/2 = 15 edges.

  3. Because all edges have equal weight, any spanning tree is an MST.

  4. Use Cayley’s formula: the number of distinct spanning trees of the complete graph on n vertices is n^{n-2}.

  5. Compute for n = 6: 6^{6-2} = 6^4 = 1296.

Answer: 1296 minimum spanning trees.

text:
Consider the following graph G.

Find the number of minimum cost spanning trees using Kruskal’s algorithm or Prim’s algorithm.
solution:
Concept: When several equal-weight edges compete during Kruskal's algorithm, the minimum total weight is still unique, but the SET of edges chosen among a tie can vary. Counting distinct minimum spanning trees means counting, at each weight tier, how many ways the tied edges can be chosen without creating a cycle.

  1. The unique smallest edge is (a, d) with weight 5. It is forced into every MST, merging a and d into one component.

  2. Both weight-6 edges, (a, b) and (b, e), connect distinct components without forming a cycle, so both are forced as well. The component is now {a, b, d, e}.

  3. Vertices c and f are still outside this component. Edge (d, e) also has weight 7, but both its endpoints already sit inside {a, b, d, e}, so it would only close a cycle and is skipped. The weight-7 edges that can actually extend the tree are (b, c), (c, e), (c, f), and (e, f).

  4. Two of these four edges are needed to bring in both c and f. Checking every pairing (table below) shows exactly one pairing closes a cycle; the rest are valid.

Pair of weight-7 edges

Connects c and f without a cycle?

(b,c) + (c,e)

No — recreates cycle b–c–e–b through the existing (b,e) edge

(b,c) + (c,f)

Yes

(b,c) + (e,f)

Yes

(c,e) + (c,f)

Yes

(c,e) + (e,f)

Yes

(c,f) + (e,f)

Yes

The remaining edge (b, d) has weight 9 — higher than every weight-7 edge — so it never appears in a minimum spanning tree.

title: Which of the following statement is false about Prim’s algorithm?
subject: Algorithm
text: Which of the following statement is false about Prim’s algorithm?

options.html: Initially the root's key is initialized to 0 and all other nodes to infinity
It may use binomial max heap to represent the priority queue
The complexity is O(E log V) using binary heap
The time complexity is O(E + V log V) using Fibonacci Heap

solution:
Concept: Prim's algorithm grows a Minimum Spanning Tree from a start vertex by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge that crosses from the tree to a vertex outside it (the cut property). To pick that cheapest crossing edge fast, every vertex keeps a key = the smallest edge weight connecting it to the current tree, and these keys are stored in a min-priority queue so that extract-min always returns the next vertex to attach.

Initialization: every vertex starts with key = infinity, then the start (root) vertex's key is set to 0 so it is the first one extracted. So the root's key is 0 while all other vertices begin at infinity and are lowered as cheaper edges are discovered.

Application — checking each statement against this method:

  • "binomial max heap for the priority queue" — Prim's needs the MINIMUM-weight vertex each step, which a min-priority queue (min-heap) provides. A max-heap returns the largest key, so it cannot drive Prim's; this claim does not hold.

  • "root key initialized to 0" — consistent with the initialization above: the start vertex's key is set to 0 (others are infinity), so this holds.

  • "O(E log V) using a binary heap" — with a binary heap each of the O(E) decrease-key and O(V) extract-min operations costs O(log V), giving O(E log V); this holds.

  • "O(E + V log V) using a Fibonacci heap" — a Fibonacci heap does decrease-key in O(1) amortized and extract-min in O(log V) amortized, giving O(E + V log V); this holds.

Cross-check: three statements match standard Prim's behaviour, so the single statement that is false about Prim's algorithm is the one claiming a binomial max heap can represent the priority queue.

optionFeedback.html: This is the standard initialization: the start (root) vertex's key is set to 0 so it is extracted first, while every other vertex starts at infinity and is lowered only when a connecting edge is found. With the root at 0 and all others at infinity, this describes exactly how Prim's begins.

A max heap (binomial or binary) always surfaces the LARGEST key, but each Prim's step needs the vertex with the SMALLEST connecting-edge weight. Choosing largest-first would attach the most expensive edges and never build a minimum spanning tree, so a max heap cannot represent this priority queue.

With a binary min-heap, Prim's performs up to O(V) extract-min and O(E) decrease-key operations, each O(log V), which sums to O(E log V) on a connected graph. This is the standard binary-heap running time.

A Fibonacci heap improves decrease-key to O(1) amortized while extract-min stays O(log V) amortized, so the E decrease-key operations contribute O(E) and the V extract-min operations contribute O(V log V), giving O(E + V log V). This is the standard Fibonacci-heap running time.

title: Which of the following algorithms is not used for finding
subject: Algorithm
text: Which of the following algorithms is not used for finding a Minimum Spanning Tree?
solution:
Concept

A Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of a connected, weighted, undirected graph is a subset of edges that connects all vertices with the minimum possible total edge weight and contains no cycle. MST algorithms grow or prune a single tree/forest using a cut or cycle rule. This is a fundamentally different problem from the shortest-path problem, which finds the minimum-weight path between vertices and may use negative-weight edges.

Application

Classify each offered algorithm by the problem it solves:

  • Kruskal's Algorithm: builds the MST by adding the globally cheapest edge that does not form a cycle (greedy on sorted edges) - an MST algorithm.

  • Prim's Algorithm: grows the MST from a start vertex, repeatedly adding the cheapest edge leaving the current tree - an MST algorithm.

  • Boruvka's Algorithm: repeatedly adds, for every component, its cheapest outgoing edge, merging components in parallel rounds - an MST algorithm.

  • Reverse-Delete Algorithm: starts from the full edge set and deletes the most expensive edges whose removal keeps the graph connected - an MST algorithm.

  • Bellman-Ford Algorithm: computes single-source shortest paths and can handle negative edge weights - a SHORTEST-PATH algorithm, not an MST algorithm.

Four of the five listed methods construct a minimum spanning tree; the remaining one solves the shortest-path problem. Hence the algorithm not used for finding an MST is Bellman-Ford.

Cross-check

MST algorithms output a set of edges forming a tree spanning all vertices; their correctness rests on the cut property (the cheapest edge crossing any cut is safe) or the cycle property (a strictly heaviest edge on any cycle is unsafe). Bellman-Ford instead outputs a shortest-path distance/predecessor table from one source and is the standard choice when negative weights are present - confirming it belongs to the shortest-path family, not the MST family.

optionFeedback.html: Kruskal's algorithm builds a spanning tree by greedily adding the smallest-weight edge that avoids a cycle, so it is in fact a standard method for constructing an MST - it does not fit a question asking which one is not used for MST.

Prim's algorithm grows a tree from a starting vertex by repeatedly taking the cheapest edge that leaves the current tree, which makes it a classic MST construction method rather than one excluded from MST work.
Boruvka's algorithm merges components by adding each component's cheapest outgoing edge in parallel rounds; this is one of the oldest MST algorithms, so it is used for finding an MST.

Bellman-Ford solves the single-source shortest-path problem - it finds minimum-weight paths from one source vertex and outputs a distance/predecessor table (it can also handle negative edge weights). This is a different optimization goal from a minimum spanning tree, which minimizes the total weight of a tree spanning all vertices. Because it targets shortest paths rather than building an MST, it is the algorithm here that is not used for MST.

The reverse-delete algorithm starts from all edges and removes the heaviest edges whose deletion keeps the graph connected, ending with an MST; it is therefore a genuine MST method, not one excluded from MST construction.

title: In the context of minimum spanning trees, the "cut property"
subject: Algorithm
text: In minimum spanning trees, the cut property is used to justify Prim's algorithm. What does the cut property state?

options.html: A maximum-weight edge in the graph must be part of every MST.
A minimum-weight edge in the graph is the only edge Prim's algorithm can choose.
A minimum-weight edge crossing the current cut is safe to add to an MST.
A maximum-weight edge crossing a cut is safe to add to an MST.

solution:
CONCEPT

A cut partitions the vertices of a connected, weighted, undirected graph into two non-empty sets. A crossing edge has one endpoint on each side of that partition.

The cut property says that a lightest edge crossing a cut is safe for the minimum spanning tree: it can be included in some MST. When all edge weights are distinct, that crossing edge is forced into the MST.

APPLICATION

  1. In Prim's algorithm, the vertices already in the growing tree form one side of a cut, and the remaining vertices form the other side.

  2. The candidate edges are the edges crossing that current cut.

  3. Choosing a minimum-weight crossing edge is safe, so adding it preserves the possibility of completing a minimum spanning tree.

  4. Therefore, the cut-property statement that fits Prim's algorithm is: a minimum-weight edge crossing the current cut is safe to add to an MST.

CONTRAST

  • A maximum-weight edge rule can add unnecessary cost and is not justified by the MST cut property.

  • A globally minimum-edge rule misses the cut restriction used in Prim's step-by-step growth.

  • A maximum-weight crossing-edge rule keeps the cut setting but reverses the light-edge condition.

RESULT

The answer is: a minimum-weight edge crossing the current cut is safe to add to an MST.

optionFeedback.html: This gives priority to a maximum-weight edge. A heavy edge is not protected by the MST greedy proof merely because its weight is large, so this rule can increase the total spanning-tree cost.
This overgeneralizes the idea of a light edge. The cut property is not an unconditional rule to pick the globally smallest edge from the whole graph at every step.
The value describes the safe-edge rule used while Prim's algorithm grows a tree: the chosen edge is the lightest available connection across the current boundary.
This treats a costly crossing edge as safe merely because it crosses the cut. Crossing the cut alone does not justify adding an edge to a minimum spanning tree.

title: Assume Dijkstra Algo is used to find shortest path, find
subject: Algorithm
text:
Assume Dijkstra's algorithm is run on the graph below, starting from source vertex G, to find the shortest path from G to every other vertex.

Find the number of edges in the graph that are NOT used in the resulting shortest-path tree.
solution:
Dijkstra's algorithm finds, from one chosen source vertex, the shortest distance to every other vertex: starting from the source, it repeatedly picks the nearest unvisited vertex and relaxes — attempts to improve — its neighbours' tentative distances. An edge becomes part of the shortest-path tree only if it ends up as a vertex's FINAL shortest-distance predecessor at the moment that vertex is finalized; an edge that is tried during relaxation but is later superseded by a shorter route (and so never becomes any vertex's final predecessor) remains unused, along with every edge that plays no role in relaxation at all.

Applying this to the given graph with source G:

  1. Initial distances from G: G = 0, A = 2 (via G–A), T = 3 (via G–T), M = 5 (via G–M), E = ∞.

  2. Pick the nearest unvisited node A (distance 2). Update neighbors: E via A = 2 + 7 = 9, M via A = 2 + 6 = 8 (no improvement to M).

  3. Pick the next nearest unvisited node T (distance 3). Update neighbors: E via T = 3 + 4 = 7 (improves E), M via T = 3 + 4 = 7 (no improvement to M since M = 5).

  4. Pick M (distance 5). Its neighbors do not improve any distances (E via M = 10 > 7). Finally pick E (distance 7).

The edges chosen when each node received its final shortest distance form the shortest-path tree:

  • Used edges in the shortest-path tree: G–A, G–T, G–M, T–E

  • All edges in the graph: G–A, A–E, E–T, T–G, G–M, A–M, E–M, T–M

  • Unused edges = (all edges) − (used edges) = A–E, A–M, E–M, T–M

Cross-check: a shortest-path tree spanning all 5 vertices (G, A, T, M, E) must contain exactly 5 − 1 = 4 edges, since any spanning tree on n vertices has n − 1 edges — this matches the 4 tree edges found above, confirming the tree is complete and correctly formed.

Count: the graph has 8 edges in total; the shortest-path tree uses 4 of them, so 8 − 4 = 4 edges are not used. The correct answer is 4.

optionFeedback.html: Running Dijkstra's algorithm from source G, the shortest-path tree is built from the edges G–A (weight 2), G–T (3), G–M (5) and T–E (4) — the four edges through which A, T, M and E each receive their final shortest distance from G. Since the graph has 8 edges in total, the remaining 4 edges never get used to finalize any vertex's shortest distance in this tree.

This total would follow from an incomplete run of Dijkstra's algorithm — for example, stopping the trace before every vertex reachable from G has actually been finalized. Complete the full trace before concluding how many of the graph's edges go unused.

This total would follow from an even more incomplete run of Dijkstra's algorithm — for example, stopping the trace right after the very first vertex beyond the source is finalized. Complete the full trace, finalizing every vertex reachable from G, before concluding how many of the graph's edges go unused.

This would follow only if the graph's edges were miscounted — for example, treating the graph as having a different total number of edges than it actually shows. Recount every edge in the diagram directly, one by one, before concluding that no listed value applies.

title: If there is cycle in graph that is reachable from
subject: Algorithm
text: If there is a cycle in a graph that is reachable from source then Dijkastra’s shortest-path algorithm may relax an edge more than once in the graph ?
solution:
Answer: False

Explanation: In the standard Dijkstra algorithm implementation that uses decrease-key, each vertex is finalized (settled) when it is extracted from the priority queue. A finalized vertex is processed exactly once, and its outgoing edges are relaxed at that time. Therefore each edge is relaxed at most once, so a reachable cycle does not cause repeated relaxations of the same edge.

  • Key idea: a vertex is given its final shortest-path distance when popped from the priority queue and is not reprocessed.

  • Outgoing edges are relaxed only when their source vertex is settled, so each edge is considered at most once in that step.

  • Cycles reachable from the source do not change this property.

  • Note: Dijkstra requires non-negative edge weights; with negative weights the algorithm is not valid.

Implementation note: Some implementations that avoid decrease-key insert duplicate entries for a vertex into the priority queue and may examine a vertex multiple times before ignoring stale entries. That is an implementation detail; the standard correctness argument relies on settling each vertex once, which prevents repeated effective relaxations due to cycles.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Dijkstra's algorithm (in the standard decrease-key implementation) finalizes each vertex when it is extracted from the priority queue; a finalized vertex is processed exactly once and its outgoing edges are relaxed at that time. Therefore a reachable cycle does not cause an edge to be relaxed more than once. Also note Dijkstra requires non-negative edge weights.

Correct. In the standard implementation using decrease-key, each vertex is settled when it is extracted from the priority queue and processed exactly once; its outgoing edges are relaxed at that time, so each edge is relaxed at most once. Dijkstra assumes non-negative edge weights.

Incorrect. The presence of a reachable cycle alone does not cause multiple relaxations in the standard Dijkstra implementation because vertices are settled once. Some non-standard implementations that avoid decrease-key and push duplicate entries into the priority queue may examine a vertex multiple times, but the standard algorithm still guarantees each edge is relaxed at most once when its source is finalized.

Incorrect. This choice is not helpful—there is a definite answer: False. Dijkstra finalizes each vertex once (in the decrease-key implementation), so reachable cycles do not cause edges to be relaxed more than once. Also remind that Dijkstra requires non-negative weights.

Incorrect. Depth-first search (DFS) follows one path as deep as possible before backtracking and does not explore vertices by increasing distance from the source. Because of that, DFS does not guarantee shortest paths even when all edges have equal weight.

Incorrect. Not all the listed algorithms behave like Dijkstra here because depth-first search does not produce shortest paths. Since DFS is not equivalent, the statement that all of the above behave identically is false.

title: Which data structure is used to maintain the distance of
subject: Algorithm
text: Which data structure is used to maintain the distance of each node in a Dijkstra’s algorithm?
solution:
Answer: Priority queue (min-priority queue).

Explanation: Dijkstra’s algorithm repeatedly selects the vertex with the smallest tentative distance and updates neighbors. A min-priority queue efficiently supports selecting the minimum-distance vertex each time.

  • Key operations: extract-min (remove the node with smallest tentative distance).

  • Key operations: decrease-key (update a node’s tentative distance when a shorter path is found).

  • Key operations: insert (add nodes into the priority queue as needed).

Implementation note: A binary min-heap is a common implementation (giving about O((V+E) log V) time). Using a Fibonacci heap improves decrease-key and yields O(E + V log V) in the theoretical bound.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. A stack uses last-in, first-out order and cannot efficiently select the node with the smallest tentative distance. Dijkstra’s algorithm needs to repeatedly extract the node with the minimum tentative distance, which is why a min-priority queue is used instead.

Incorrect. A simple FIFO queue processes nodes in insertion order, not by smallest tentative distance. Dijkstra’s algorithm requires extracting the node with the smallest tentative distance each step, so a min-priority queue is required for efficient selection.

Correct. Dijkstra’s algorithm maintains tentative distances in a min-priority queue so it can efficiently extract the node with the smallest tentative distance at each step. Typical operations used are extract-min and decrease-key; common implementations use a binary min-heap or a Fibonacci heap for better decrease-key performance.

Incorrect. A generic tree structure does not provide efficient operations to repeatedly select and update the node with the smallest tentative distance. A min-priority queue (min-heap) is the appropriate structure for those operations in Dijkstra’s algorithm.

title: In the Dijkstra algorithm the shortest path always passes through
subject: Algorithm
text: In the Dijkstra algorithm the shortest path always passes through the least number of vertices?
solution:
Answer: false — Dijkstra finds the path with minimum total edge weight, not the path that passes through the fewest vertices.

Why: Dijkstra's objective is to minimize the sum of edge weights along a path. The count of intermediate vertices is not considered, so a path with more vertices can have a smaller total weight than a shorter path in terms of vertex count.

  • Counterexample: vertices A, B, C with edges A–B weight 5, B–C weight 5, and A–C weight 15.

  • From A to C, the path A→B→C has total weight 10 and uses three vertices, while the direct path A→C has total weight 15 and uses two vertices. Dijkstra picks A→B→C because its total weight is smaller, even though it visits more vertices.

Note: Dijkstra requires non-negative edge weights. If negative-weight edges are present, use an algorithm designed for that case (for example, Bellman-Ford).

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Dijkstra finds paths that minimize the total sum of edge weights, not the number of vertices visited. A path with fewer vertices can have a larger total weight than a longer path; Dijkstra picks the smaller-weight path. Also note Dijkstra assumes non-negative edge weights.

Correct. Dijkstra minimizes total path weight (sum of edge weights), not the number of vertices. For example, if there is a direct edge of weight 15 between two nodes but a two-edge route of weights 5 and 5, the two-edge route (which visits more vertices) has smaller total weight and is chosen. Also remember Dijkstra requires non-negative edge weights.

Misleading. The statement is false regardless of whether negative weights exist. Dijkstra optimizes total weight, not vertex count. Separately, Dijkstra is not safe to use with negative-weight edges; for graphs with negative weights use Bellman-Ford or another appropriate algorithm.
Incorrect. The best answer is the option stating that the claim is false. Explain that Dijkstra minimizes total edge weight rather than the number of vertices, and give a short example to illustrate.

title: To implement Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm on unweighted graphs so
subject: Algorithm
text: To implement Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm on unweighted graphs so that it runs in linear time, the data structure to be used is
solution: Dijkstra's algorithm is typically used for weighted graphs and relies on a priority queue (often implemented as a heap) to efficiently select the next vertex with the smallest tentative distance. However, in unweighted graphs, every edge has a uniform weight (usually 1). This means that the order in which vertices are visited follows a simple breadth-first pattern. Instead of using a complex priority queue or heap, we can use a standard First-In-First-Out (FIFO) Queue. By processing vertices in the order they are discovered, we ensure that each vertex is visited at its minimum distance level before moving to the next. This approach effectively transforms Dijkstra's algorithm into Breadth-First Search (BFS), which runs in linear time O(V + E). A B-tree is used for database indexing and does not manage traversal order. A Stack would lead to Depth-First Search (DFS), which does not guarantee shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Therefore, a Queue is the optimal data structure for this specific scenario.

title: Which of the following is/are false?
subject: Algorithm
text: Which of the following is/are false?

options.html: For every weighted graph with starting vertex at S, Bellman Ford algorithm always gives shortest path to any given vertex V.
If a graph contains a negative weight cycle then Dijkstra’s algorithm may not terminate
For a directed graph, the absence of back edges across a complete DFS forest means there is no cycle.
A complete graph of 4 vertices can have maximum 16 minimum cost spanning trees.

solution:
Concept

A statement of the form "this algorithm/theorem always guarantees X" is false the moment it drops the precondition that the guarantee depends on. So evaluate each claim against the exact requirement of the underlying result: Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra each need a specific condition on negative weights, DFS back edges characterise directed cycles, and Cayley's formula counts spanning trees of a complete graph.

Applying it to each statement

  1. Bellman-Ford "always" for "every" weighted graph: this overstates the guarantee. Bellman-Ford returns correct shortest paths only when no negative-weight cycle is reachable from the source; with a reachable negative cycle the shortest paths are undefined and it reports the cycle instead.

  2. Dijkstra and a negative-weight cycle: the standard algorithm extracts and finalises each vertex from the priority queue exactly once, so its main loop is bounded to exactly |V| iterations on any finite graph, whatever the edge weights are. A negative cycle cannot make this loop run forever — it can only leave an already-finalised vertex holding a distance that a later relaxation along the cycle would have lowered further, so the reported distances come out wrong while the algorithm itself still halts. The claim that it 'may not terminate' overstates what a negative cycle actually breaks: correctness fails here, not termination.

  3. DFS back edges in a directed graph: a back edge points to an ancestor on the recursion stack and exists exactly when a directed cycle exists, so no back edges across the DFS forest means the graph is acyclic.

  4. Spanning trees of K4: Cayley's formula gives n(n-2) spanning trees, i.e. 42 = 16; with all edge weights equal, every one of these 16 trees is a minimum-cost spanning tree.

Cross-check

The over-general guarantees are the false ones; the structural facts (DFS back-edge characterisation, Cayley count) hold exactly as stated.

optionFeedback.html: Bellman-Ford computes shortest paths only when there is no negative-weight cycle reachable from the start vertex. The blanket guarantee "for every weighted graph" ignores this condition: when a negative-weight cycle is reachable, the shortest paths are undefined and Bellman-Ford reports the negative cycle instead of returning valid distances.

The standard formulation of Dijkstra's algorithm removes and finalises each vertex from the priority queue exactly once, so its main loop is bounded to exactly |V| iterations on any finite graph, whatever the edge weights are. A negative-weight cycle cannot make this loop run forever — it can only leave an already-finalised vertex holding a distance that a later relaxation along the cycle would have lowered further, so the reported distances come out wrong while the algorithm still halts. A negative cycle breaks correctness, not termination.

In a directed graph a back edge during depth-first search is an edge to an ancestor still on the recursion stack, and such an edge exists exactly when a directed cycle exists. So if the DFS forest produces no back edge, every directed cycle is ruled out and the graph is acyclic.

By Cayley's formula a complete graph on n vertices has n(n-2) spanning trees; for n = 4 that is 42 = 16. When every edge has the same weight, each of those spanning trees has equal total cost, so all 16 are simultaneously minimum-cost spanning trees.

title: Which of the following statements are incorrect: Adding number on
subject: Algorithm
text:
Which of the following statements are incorrect:

S1: Adding a number on every edge of a graph may change the shortest path.

S2: A graph where all edge weights are distinct can have more than one shortest path between two vertices.
solution:
Answer: None of the statements is incorrect; both statements are correct.

  • Explanation for the first statement: Adding the same constant to every edge can change which path is shortest. This is because each path’s total increases by (constant × number of edges in that path), so paths with different edge counts can swap order after the addition.

    Example: Path X uses two edges of weights 1 and 1 (total 2). Path Y uses a single edge of weight 3 (total 3). Initially Path X is shorter (2 < 3). If we add 2 to every edge, Path X becomes 6 and Path Y becomes 5, so the shortest path changes.

  • Explanation for the second statement: Distinct individual edge weights do not guarantee a unique shortest path. Different combinations of distinct weights can sum to the same total, producing multiple shortest paths.

    Example: Edges with weights 1, 4, and 5 are all distinct. One path could use edges of weights 1 and 4 (total 5), while another path could use the single edge of weight 5 (total 5). Both paths tie as shortest.

Conclusion: Since both statements are true, none of them is incorrect.

This choice claims both statements are incorrect. Both statements are actually correct: adding the same number to every edge can change the shortest path (because path lengths shift by the number of edges), and distinct edge weights do not prevent two different paths from having equal total weight. Therefore this choice is incorrect.

This choice says none of the two statements are incorrect. That is correct. The first statement is true because adding the same constant to every edge changes a path's total cost by (constant × number of edges), which can change which path is shortest. The second statement is also true because distinct individual edge weights do not forbid two different paths from having the same total weight (sums of distinct numbers can coincide).

This choice claims only the second statement is incorrect. The second statement is actually correct: even if every edge in the graph has a distinct weight, two different paths can still sum to the same total weight (so there can be more than one shortest path). Therefore this choice is incorrect.

Reason:

  • Bellman–Ford relaxes every edge in the graph for V-1 iterations to compute shortest paths. Each iteration scans all E edges, so these passes cost O((V-1)·E) = O(VE).

title: Graph is such that every vertex is connected to every
subject: Algorithm
text: A complete graph G has a direct edge between every pair of distinct vertices. If Bellman–Ford is used to find a shortest path, what is its asymptotic running time in terms of V, the number of vertices?
solution:
Concept: For any weighted graph (including ones with negative edge weights), Bellman–Ford's running time is the product of two governing quantities: the number of relaxation rounds, V − 1, and the work per round, which relaxes every edge once, i.e. Θ(E). This gives the general bound O(V × E), valid regardless of how many edges the graph has.

Application:

  1. Per-round work: every edge is relaxed once per round, costing Θ(E).

  2. Number of rounds: V − 1, so multiplying the two gives a total of O(V × E).

  3. Edge count for this graph: G is complete, so every distinct pair of vertices has an edge. The exact count is V(V−1)/2 — for V = 4 that is 4×3/2 = 6, not 42 = 16, so the exact count and 'V2' are not the same number.

  4. Asymptotic order of that count: Big-Θ notation describes growth rate, not an exact value at one V. As V grows, V(V−1)/2 grows in proportion to V2 (the −1 and the 1/2 factor don't change the growth rate), so we write E = Θ(V2) — meaning 'grows like V2', not 'equals V2 exactly'. That is why 6 (the true edge count at V = 4) and 16 (literally V2 at V = 4) can both be consistent with E = Θ(V2).

  5. Substituting E = Θ(V2) into the general bound O(V × E) gives O(V × V2) = O(V3), the running time for Bellman–Ford's shortest-path search on this complete graph.

Cross-check: Doubling V roughly quadruples the exact edge count V(V−1)/2, consistent with quadratic growth, which confirms E = Θ(V2) is the right order to substitute. A final extra round to detect negative-weight cycles costs one more Θ(E) pass and does not change this asymptotic bound. Note also that if all edge weights were guaranteed non-negative, a priority-queue-based algorithm could run faster in practice — but Bellman–Ford is needed precisely because it correctly handles negative edge weights, which a plain priority-queue approach cannot.

optionFeedback.html: O(V³) is a cubic vertex-count bound: replacing V by 2V multiplies its leading growth term by 8.
O(V²) is a quadratic vertex-count bound: replacing V by 2V multiplies its leading growth term by 4.
O(V + E log V) combines a term linear in V with an edge-processing term that has a logarithmic factor in V.
“None of the above” is a set-level assertion that every displayed asymptotic expression is excluded.

title: Given Graph, Assume that if it takes time to travel
subject: Algorithm
text:
Given Graph, Assume that if it takes time T to travel from vertex a to b, then it takes the same time to travel from b to a. We wish to select a walk from vertex 1 to some other vertex, back to vertex 1 and so on till each vertex (except vertex 1 - the source) is visited exactly once.

Let the initial instant be T= 0. Let the times of visit of vertices 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 from T = 0 be T2, T3, T4 , T5, T6 and T7. We wish to minimise the sum of T2, T3, T4, T5, T6 and T7. Find out the minimum possible sum of the given times [ Note: Each edge cost is nothing but travel time] ______
solution:
Corrected reasoning and final calculation:

Key idea: Each visit to a vertex starts at vertex 1, and between consecutive visits we return to vertex 1. For the k-th vertex visited (in the chosen order) its arrival time equals the sum of all previous round trips plus the one-way travel to this vertex. This makes earlier chosen edges contribute more to the total sum, so assign smaller edge times to earlier visits.

Derivation of coefficients for six vertices:

  • If the chosen visit order has edge times w1,w2,w3,w4,w5,w6, the arrival times sum to:

  • w1 + (2w1 + w2) + (2w1 + 2w2 + w3) + ... + (2w1 + 2w2 + 2w3 + 2w4 + 2w5 + w6).

Thus the coefficients multiplying w1..w6 are 11, 9, 7, 5, 3, 1 respectively. To minimize the total, sort edge times in ascending order and assign them to these coefficients in that order (smallest time gets coefficient 11, next smallest gets 9, and so on).

Edge times from vertex 1 to each vertex (from the diagram):

  • Vertex 2: 2

  • Vertex 3: 5

  • Vertex 4: 3

  • Vertex 5: 7

  • Vertex 6: 8

  • Vertex 7: 6

Assigning coefficients and computing the sum:

  • 5 × 6 = 30

  • 3 × 7 = 21

Total minimum sum = 22 + 27 + 35 + 30 + 21 + 8 = 143.

title: Match the following: Floyd Warshall shortest path between two vertices
subject: Algorithm
text:
Match the following:

(A) Floyd Warshall

(i) shortest path between two vertices

(B) Dijkstra

(ii) single source shortest path

(C) Kruskal's

(iii) Minimum spanning tree

(D) Bellman ford

(iv) solving all pair shortest path
solution:
Concept

A graph problem fixes which shortest-path or tree algorithm fits. Three families decide every match: an all-pairs shortest-path algorithm finds the shortest distance between every ordered pair of vertices at once; a single-source shortest-path algorithm fixes one source and finds shortest paths from it to all others (and so also to any one target vertex); and a minimum-spanning-tree algorithm connects all vertices with minimum total edge weight, which is not a shortest-path task at all.

Applying it to each item

  1. Floyd-Warshall runs a dynamic program over all intermediate vertices, so it returns shortest distances for every pair simultaneously - it is the all-pairs shortest path algorithm, matching "solving all pair shortest path".

  2. Kruskal's algorithm greedily adds the lightest safe edge without forming a cycle, building a minimum-weight tree that spans all vertices - it matches "Minimum spanning tree".

  3. Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges from a single chosen source and also handles negative edge weights - it matches "single source shortest path".

  4. Dijkstra is also a single-source method (for non-negative weights), but in this forced one-to-one matching the "single source shortest path" target is already taken by Bellman-Ford, so Dijkstra takes the remaining "shortest path between two vertices" - which it can do by stopping once the target vertex is settled.

Cross-check

Only one assignment makes every pairing factually defensible at once: Floyd-Warshall = all-pairs, Kruskal = MST, Bellman-Ford = single-source, Dijkstra = path between two vertices. Any pairing that calls Floyd-Warshall a two-vertex method, or makes Bellman-Ford all-pairs, or links Dijkstra to a spanning tree, breaks on a definition, so the matching above is the consistent one.

optionFeedback.html: This puts Floyd-Warshall on a spanning-tree task and Kruskal's on a shortest-path task, but Floyd-Warshall computes shortest distances while Kruskal's builds a spanning tree - their roles are swapped, so this pairing contradicts what each algorithm does.

Here Floyd-Warshall sits on all-pairs shortest path, Kruskal's on minimum spanning tree, and Bellman-Ford on single-source shortest path - each on the task it is actually built for. With the single-source target taken by Bellman-Ford, Dijkstra falls to shortest path between two vertices, which it reaches by stopping once that target vertex is settled.

This treats Floyd-Warshall as a two-vertex method and casts Bellman-Ford as an all-pairs method. Floyd-Warshall is not limited to a single pair, and Bellman-Ford works outward from one chosen source, so both of these placements misstate the algorithm's scope.

This calls Floyd-Warshall single-source and ties Dijkstra to a minimum spanning tree. Floyd-Warshall works over all pairs, and Dijkstra finds shortest paths rather than building a spanning tree, so these placements break on what each algorithm does.

title: Match the following table showing algorithm and its application. Scenarios
subject: Algorithm
text:

Scenarios

Algorithms

(R) All N persons wants to visit all M places in shortest period

solution:
Concept

Shortest-path algorithms are distinguished by the query model and graph structure. Floyd–Warshall precomputes all-pairs distances, Dijkstra handles non-negative weighted single-source queries and can be repeated for several sources, and the multi-stage graph method uses the layered structure of a directed acyclic graph.

A matching question must therefore be read using the particular operational interpretation adopted by its source examination.

Application

  1. For P, the official ISRO interpretation uses Floyd’s algorithm: an all-pairs distance table can answer a requested place-to-place query.

  2. For Q, the visit through M places is interpreted as movement through successive stages, so it is paired with the multi-stage graph algorithm.

  3. For R, Dijkstra’s algorithm is interpreted as being run from each relevant person’s starting vertex to obtain routes to the M destinations, assuming non-negative edge weights.

Cross-check

  • The revised final ISRO Computer Science answer key for the 2025 A-series Question 37 selects the mapping P–(i), Q–(ii), R–(iii).

  • The wording is not algorithmically exclusive: Dijkstra can also answer a single source-to-destination query, while Floyd–Warshall is the direct all-pairs method. The accepted mapping here follows the official PYQ key rather than claiming those alternatives are impossible.

Therefore, the officially accepted matching is P–(i), Q–(ii), R–(iii).

title: Consider weighted undirected graph with positive edge weights and let
subject: Algorithm
text: Consider a weighted undirected graph with positive edge weights and let (u, v) be an edge in the graph. It is known that the shortest path from source vertex s to u has weight 53 and shortest path from s to v has weight 65. Which statement is always true?
solution: In a weighted graph, the shortest path distance satisfies the triangle inequality. For edge (u, v), dist(s, v) ≤ dist(s, u) + weight(u, v). Substituting the given values: 65 ≤ 53 + w. Therefore, the edge weight must be at least 12.

optionFeedback.html: This option violates the triangle inequality for shortest paths. Since the path to v is longer, the edge weight must be at least 12, not less. Check your inequality direction carefully when comparing path distances and edge weights.

While the weight must be at least 12, it is not necessarily exactly 12. The shortest path constraint establishes a lower bound rather than an exact value for the edge weight. Verify if the statement holds for all valid graph configurations.

The triangle inequality implies the edge weight must be at least the difference between path lengths, so w is greater than or equal to 12. This option incorrectly suggests strict inequality, ignoring the valid scenario where the weight equals exactly 12 while satisfying all shortest path constraints.

The triangle inequality enforces a lower bound on edge weights based on path differences, specifically requiring w to be at least 12. This option permits values less than 12, which would create a shorter path to v than the known shortest distance of 65.

title: Arrange the following algorithms from the most efficient to least
subject: Algorithm
text:
Arrange the following algorithms from the most efficient to least efficient using their standard worst-case time complexities:

  • A. Kruskal's Algorithm

  • B. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

  • C. Bellman-Ford Algorithm

  • D. Dijkstra's Algorithm

  • E. Edmonds-Karp Algorithm

Choose the correct sequence.
solution:
Correct sequence: B, D, A, C, E.

  • BFS: O(V + E), usually the lightest among the listed algorithms.

  • Dijkstra: commonly O((V + E) log V) with a priority queue for non-negative weighted graphs.

  • Kruskal: O(E log E), mainly due to sorting edges.

  • Bellman-Ford: O(VE).

  • Edmonds-Karp: O(VE²), which is heavier than Bellman-Ford.

So the order from most efficient to least efficient is B, D, A, C, E.

Correct. BFS is lightest, followed by Dijkstra and Kruskal under common comparisons; Bellman-Ford O(VE) comes before Edmonds-Karp O(VE²).

This is not correct. Bellman-Ford should not come immediately after BFS, and Dijkstra should not be placed last because its usual priority-queue complexity is lower than Bellman-Ford and Edmonds-Karp.

title: Which of the following algorithms use Greedy strategy? Dijkstra’s algorithm
subject: Algorithm
text:
Which of the following algorithms use Greedy strategy?
A. Dijkstra’s algorithm
B. Kruskal’s algorithm
C. Huffman coding
D. Bellman-Ford algorithm
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
Answer: Dijkstra’s algorithm, Kruskal’s algorithm, and Huffman coding.

Explanation:

  • Dijkstra’s algorithm: Greedy. At each step it selects the vertex with the smallest tentative distance and finalizes that choice, never needing to revise it.

  • Kruskal’s algorithm: Greedy. It repeatedly picks the smallest-weight edge that does not create a cycle, making locally optimal edge choices to build a minimum spanning forest.

  • Huffman coding: Greedy. It repeatedly merges the two least-frequent symbols to build an optimal prefix code, making a locally optimal merge at each step.

  • Bellman-Ford algorithm: Not greedy. It uses repeated relaxation of edges and can update previously made choices based on information found later, which is characteristic of dynamic programming/iterative relaxation rather than a greedy one-pass choice.

Therefore the correct set of algorithms that use a greedy strategy is Dijkstra’s algorithm, Kruskal’s algorithm, and Huffman coding.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. This choice includes Bellman-Ford, which is not a greedy algorithm. Bellman-Ford repeatedly relaxes edges and may revisit and update distances based on paths found later, so it does not follow a one-pass greedy choice property. The correct set should include Huffman coding instead of Bellman-Ford.

Correct. Dijkstra’s algorithm, Kruskal’s algorithm, and Huffman coding use a greedy strategy: Dijkstra picks the nearest unreached vertex at each step, Kruskal repeatedly selects the smallest-weight edge that doesn't form a cycle, and Huffman repeatedly merges the two least-frequent symbols. Bellman-Ford is not greedy because it uses repeated relaxation and can update choices based on later information.
